sources.title: The Duration of the Repeated-Bout Effect After Eccentric Exercise
sources.authors: Theodorou AA, Margaritelis NV, Karyofyllidou AV, Christodoulou F, Jamurtas AZ, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 48 recreationally active young men with no muscle-damaging exercise in the prior 6 months; four independent groups repeated the same maximal eccentric knee-extensor bout (5 x 15 at 60 deg/s) after 3, 6, 9 or 12 weeks; outcomes before and on days 2 and 4 (Scand J Med Sci Sports 2026;36(10):e70381).
sources.findings: The prior bout attenuated damage markers at 3 and 6 weeks across most outcomes and for selected markers at 9 weeks; at 12 weeks no difference, with exploratory equivalence for torque, range of motion, soreness, thickness and echo intensity (CK and hs-CRP inconclusive). The authors suggest periodic eccentric stimuli while avoiding excessive muscle damage close to important competitions.
sources.locator: Europe PMC full text PMC13674372 (JATS) read by this instance for R7B1-SSCTR-r1, the same day: Abstract, 2.1-2.4, Results (equivalence), Discussion (practical implications, limitations).
limitations: Young men, one muscle group, a maximal laboratory protocol far heavier than a 1-set establishment dose; days 2 and 4 only; equivalence margins post hoc.
counterevidence: Elbow-flexor studies cited by the authors report longer protection; a 1-set dose at RIR 3-4 is unlikely to cause the damage of a maximal eccentric bout.

sources.title: Prevention of downhill walking-induced muscle damage by non-damaging downhill walking.
sources.authors: Maeo S, Yamamoto M, Kanehisa H, Nosaka K.
sources.population_design_dose: Untrained young men allocated (n = 12/group) to control, 5 min of downhill walking (-28%, 5 km/h, 10% body-mass load) or 5 min of level walking one week before 40 min of downhill walking; knee-extensor strength, CK and soreness before and 24-72 h after (PLoS One 2017;12(3):e0173909).
sources.findings: The 5-min bouts changed no marker. After the 40-min bout the control and level-walking groups lost about 19% of strength with high CK and soreness, while the 5-min downhill group was attenuated by 47-64% (strength -9.9%, CK 339 U/L, soreness 28 mm): a non-damaging bout of the same task protected; a different, less eccentric task did not.
sources.locator: Europe PMC full text PMC5348007 read by this instance for R7B1-SSCTR-r1, the same day: Abstract, Introduction, Materials and methods (DW and LW), Results, Discussion.
limitations: Young untrained men; downhill walking, not resistance exercise; one-week interval; allocation method not described as randomized in the text read; small groups.
counterevidence: Protection from the light bout was partial, not complete.

sources.title: The repeated bout effect of traditional resistance training on cycling efficiency and performance.
sources.authors: Devantier-Thomas B, Deakin GB, Crowther F, Schumann M, Doma K.
sources.population_design_dose: Ten resistance-untrained male cyclists (38 +/- 13 y); two identical lower-body resistance sessions (3 x 6 at 95% of 6RM: Smith squat, single-leg press, leg extension, leg curl) at least two weeks apart; markers and cycling tests before, 24 h and 48 h after each (Eur J Appl Physiol 2024;124(7):2005-2017).
sources.findings: Soreness was lower after the second bout (24 h 4.8 vs 6.4; 48 h 4.5 vs 6.3 on a 10-point scale); jump height fell and RPE at 90% of VT2 rose 24-48 h after the sessions; 10-km time trial unchanged.
sources.locator: Europe PMC full text PMC11199296 read by this instance for R7B1-SSCTR-r1, the same day: Abstract, Methods (participants, design, resistance bout), Results (Tables 2-4).
limitations: n = 10 men; cyclists, not runners; heavy loads; two bouts only; no control group.
counterevidence: Time-trial performance was maintained after both bouts.

sources.title: Acute Neuromuscular, Physiological and Performance Responses After Strength Training in Runners: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: de Carvalho e Silva GI, Brandao LHA, dos Santos Silva D, de Jesus Alves MD, Aidar FJ, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: Systematic review (19 studies) and meta-analysis (13) of acute responses of runners to a strength session, immediately to 48 h (Sports Med Open 2022;8(1):105).
sources.findings: After a strength session peak torque fell and soreness, CK and RPE rose; submaximal running physiology was largely unaffected; speed fell in two studies and time to exhaustion in all that measured it.
sources.locator: Europe PMC full text PMC9385928: abstract, key points and study selection re-read by this instance for R7B1-SSCTR-r1, the same day (read in full by the R7-B SSCTR instance in R7B-SSCTR-r1).
limitations: Few heterogeneous studies; mostly damaging protocols; no taper context.
counterevidence: Submaximal running physiology often unchanged.

sources.title: Gaining more from doing less? The effects of a one-week deload period during supervised resistance training on muscular adaptations.
sources.authors: Coleman M, Burke R, Augustin F, Piñero A, Maldonado J, Fisher JP, Israetel M, Androulakis Korakakis P, Swinton P, Oberlin D, Schoenfeld BJ.
sources.population_design_dose: RCT; 39 resistance-trained young adults (29 men, 10 women); 9-week high-volume program (lower body supervised, 5 x 8-12RM per exercise, 4 sessions/week); one group stopped all resistance training for week 5 (DELOAD), the other trained continuously (TRAD) (PeerJ 2024;12:e16777).
sources.findings: Increases in lower-body muscle thickness, local endurance and power did not differ between groups; continuous training probably gave larger strength gains (posterior probability favouring TRAD 0.85 for squat 1RM and 0.92 for isometric strength; small to large effects).
sources.locator: Europe PMC full text PMC10809978 read in this recheck: Abstract, Participants, Resistance training procedures, Results (Strength and performance, Table 1), Discussion (Strength), Limitations, Conclusion.
limitations: Young resistance-trained adults; hypertrophy-oriented protocol to failure; complete cessation of all resistance training, not one exercise or a light session; lower body only; no endurance or taper context.
counterevidence: Earlier studies cited by the authors found little or no effect of short cessation on strength (Ogasawara 2011, 2013).

literature_snapshot.counterevidence_search: Directed counterevidence: a full week without resistance training probably blunted maximal-strength gains in trained adults while muscle size, endurance and power gains were unaffected (Coleman 2024), so event-week omissions carry a small, recoverable strength cost; it is weighed against the race priority and the approved R6 event envelope, which already reduces strength and stops it in the final days. No study was found showing that a first exposure to a new strength exercise days before a race is harmless or harmful at a 1-set, RIR 3-4 dose; the protection a prior bout gives is task-specific (Maeo 2017) and wanes over 9-12 weeks (Theodorou 2026).

sources.title: Effects of tapering on performance in endurance athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.authors: Wang Z, Wang YT, Gao W, Zhong Y
sources.population_design_dose: Meta-analysis of 14 trials in well-trained endurance athletes (VO2max > 55 ml/kg/min or equivalent); tapers of 6-28 days (PLoS One 2023;18(5):e0282838).
sources.findings: Time trial improved after tapering (SMD -0.45, 95% CI -0.68 to -0.23, I2 8%); tapers of 7 days or less SMD -0.36 (-0.63 to -0.08); maintained intensity and frequency with volume cut 41-60% gave the largest effect; no VO2max or economy change.
sources.locator: Europe PMC full text PMC10171681: Results (time trial, subgroups, Table 2) re-read by this instance for R7B1-SSCTR-r1, the same day.
limitations: Well-trained athletes; no concurrent-strength data.
counterevidence: Indirect for recreational 10K and half-marathon runners.

sources.title: The Duration of the Repeated-Bout Effect After Eccentric Exercise
sources.authors: Theodorou AA, Margaritelis NV, Karyofyllidou AV, Christodoulou F, Jamurtas AZ, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 48 recreationally active young men with no muscle-damaging exercise in the prior 6 months; four independent groups repeated the same maximal eccentric knee-extensor bout (5 x 15 at 60 deg/s) after 3, 6, 9 or 12 weeks; outcomes before and on days 2 and 4 (Scand J Med Sci Sports 2026;36(10):e70381).
sources.findings: The prior bout attenuated damage markers at 3 and 6 weeks across most outcomes and for selected markers at 9 weeks; at 12 weeks no difference, with exploratory equivalence for torque, range of motion, soreness, thickness and echo intensity (CK and hs-CRP inconclusive). The authors suggest periodic eccentric stimuli while avoiding excessive muscle damage close to important competitions.
sources.locator: Europe PMC full text PMC13674372 (JATS) read by this instance for R7B1-SSCTR-r1, the same day: Abstract, 2.1-2.4, Results (equivalence), Discussion (practical implications, limitations).
limitations: Young men, one muscle group, a maximal laboratory protocol far heavier than a 1-set establishment dose; days 2 and 4 only; equivalence margins post hoc.
counterevidence: Elbow-flexor studies cited by the authors report longer protection; a 1-set dose at RIR 3-4 is unlikely to cause the damage of a maximal eccentric bout.

sources.title: Prevention of downhill walking-induced muscle damage by non-damaging downhill walking.
sources.authors: Maeo S, Yamamoto M, Kanehisa H, Nosaka K.
sources.population_design_dose: Untrained young men allocated (n = 12/group) to control, 5 min of downhill walking (-28%, 5 km/h, 10% body-mass load) or 5 min of level walking one week before 40 min of downhill walking; knee-extensor strength, CK and soreness before and 24-72 h after (PLoS One 2017;12(3):e0173909).
sources.findings: The 5-min bouts changed no marker. After the 40-min bout the control and level-walking groups lost about 19% of strength with high CK and soreness, while the 5-min downhill group was attenuated by 47-64% (strength -9.9%, CK 339 U/L, soreness 28 mm): a non-damaging bout of the same task protected; a different, less eccentric task did not.
sources.locator: Europe PMC full text PMC5348007 read by this instance for R7B1-SSCTR-r1, the same day: Abstract, Introduction, Materials and methods (DW and LW), Results, Discussion.
limitations: Young untrained men; downhill walking, not resistance exercise; one-week interval; allocation method not described as randomized in the text read; small groups.
counterevidence: Protection from the light bout was partial, not complete.

sources.title: The repeated bout effect of traditional resistance training on cycling efficiency and performance.
sources.authors: Devantier-Thomas B, Deakin GB, Crowther F, Schumann M, Doma K.
sources.population_design_dose: Ten resistance-untrained male cyclists (38 +/- 13 y); two identical lower-body resistance sessions (3 x 6 at 95% of 6RM: Smith squat, single-leg press, leg extension, leg curl) at least two weeks apart; markers and cycling tests before, 24 h and 48 h after each (Eur J Appl Physiol 2024;124(7):2005-2017).
sources.findings: Soreness was lower after the second bout (24 h 4.8 vs 6.4; 48 h 4.5 vs 6.3 on a 10-point scale); jump height fell and RPE at 90% of VT2 rose 24-48 h after the sessions; 10-km time trial unchanged.
sources.locator: Europe PMC full text PMC11199296 read by this instance for R7B1-SSCTR-r1, the same day: Abstract, Methods (participants, design, resistance bout), Results (Tables 2-4).
limitations: n = 10 men; cyclists, not runners; heavy loads; two bouts only; no control group.
counterevidence: Time-trial performance was maintained after both bouts.

sources.title: Acute Neuromuscular, Physiological and Performance Responses After Strength Training in Runners: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: de Carvalho e Silva GI, Brandao LHA, dos Santos Silva D, de Jesus Alves MD, Aidar FJ, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: Systematic review (19 studies) and meta-analysis (13) of acute responses of runners to a strength session, immediately to 48 h (Sports Med Open 2022;8(1):105).
sources.findings: After a strength session peak torque fell and soreness, CK and RPE rose; submaximal running physiology was largely unaffected; speed fell in two studies and time to exhaustion in all that measured it.
sources.locator: Europe PMC full text PMC9385928: abstract, key points and study selection re-read by this instance for R7B1-SSCTR-r1, the same day (read in full by the R7-B SSCTR instance in R7B-SSCTR-r1).
limitations: Few heterogeneous studies; mostly damaging protocols; no taper context.
counterevidence: Submaximal running physiology often unchanged.

sources.title: Gaining more from doing less? The effects of a one-week deload period during supervised resistance training on muscular adaptations.
sources.authors: Coleman M, Burke R, Augustin F, Piñero A, Maldonado J, Fisher JP, Israetel M, Androulakis Korakakis P, Swinton P, Oberlin D, Schoenfeld BJ.
sources.population_design_dose: RCT; 39 resistance-trained young adults (29 men, 10 women); 9-week high-volume program (lower body supervised, 5 x 8-12RM per exercise, 4 sessions/week); one group stopped all resistance training for week 5 (DELOAD), the other trained continuously (TRAD) (PeerJ 2024;12:e16777).
sources.findings: Increases in lower-body muscle thickness, local endurance and power did not differ between groups; continuous training probably gave larger strength gains (posterior probability favouring TRAD 0.85 for squat 1RM and 0.92 for isometric strength; small to large effects).
sources.locator: Europe PMC full text PMC10809978 read in this recheck: Abstract, Participants, Resistance training procedures, Results (Strength and performance, Table 1), Discussion (Strength), Limitations, Conclusion.
limitations: Young resistance-trained adults; hypertrophy-oriented protocol to failure; complete cessation of all resistance training, not one exercise or a light session; lower body only; no endurance or taper context.
counterevidence: Earlier studies cited by the authors found little or no effect of short cessation on strength (Ogasawara 2011, 2013).

literature_snapshot.counterevidence_search: Directed counterevidence: a full week without resistance training probably blunted maximal-strength gains in trained adults while muscle size, endurance and power gains were unaffected (Coleman 2024), so event-week omissions carry a small, recoverable strength cost; it is weighed against the race priority and the approved R6 event envelope, which already reduces strength and stops it in the final days. No study was found showing that a first exposure to a new strength exercise days before a race is harmless or harmful at a 1-set, RIR 3-4 dose; the protection a prior bout gives is task-specific (Maeo 2017) and wanes over 9-12 weeks (Theodorou 2026).

Where a configuration was never performed (missed sessions, a new equipment substitute, a rebuild or rotation row, a row the time fit dropped earlier), prescribing it in the event weeks would make its first exposure fall days before or after the race; the plan is not adequate in that respect.

The material facts are the program's execution record (the week-start state from executed sessions; intake reports do not count), the equipment of the date as the athlete reported it, and any reason-based request after the clinical screen.

KEEP of a performed configuration is defensible and is what the rule does. KEEP of a never-performed one is not, under R6-EVENT-TRANSITION C7 and B0-C05 c1. Unknown: how the individual athlete would respond to one low-dose first exposure.
A change is necessary only for the rows never performed; the comparator FREEZE-1 used, prescribing them as first exposures, breaches the event envelope.

A performed admissible configuration that fits the equipment of the date stands in at its own reduced dose; otherwise the slot, or the light session, is left out and disclosed; the configuration starts after the post-event week with establishment.

Prescribing the first exposure at a reduced dose still makes it a first exposure near the race; asking the athlete adds nothing a disclosure does not give; rewriting the session or the taper is not needed.
The event is the protected priority: no novel stimulus and no strength volume above the planned taper; strength development resumes after the event.

The rule follows the approved R6 event envelope; its direction is supported by the repeated-bout literature (Theodorou 2026, Maeo 2017, Devantier-Thomas 2024), acute strength effects in runners (de Carvalho e Silva 2022) and taper evidence (Wang 2023), and the cost of the omissions is bounded by Coleman 2024; SUPPORTED_WITH_LIMITS.
The size of the risk from one low-dose first exposure near a race is not quantified, nor is the strength cost of two to three weeks of reduced or absent exposure in recreational hybrid athletes.

The clinical screen comes first, also before any block choice: pain, injury, illness or a functional limitation routes CLINICAL_HUMAN_REQUIRED with no proposal; an unconfirmed preference or a missing reason is ASK; no HOLD is needed for the nonclinical case.

sources.population_design_dose: RCT; 839 healthy recreational runners (1-3 runs/week for 6 months); 8-week common preconditioning, then 16 weeks progressing hard-intensity volume or easy volume; 447 entered the focus period (BMJ Open Sport Exerc Med 2018;4(1):e000333).
sources.findings: Running-related injury 36 of 221 (16%) with intensity progression versus 44 of 226 (19%) with volume progression; risk differences small with confidence intervals including zero.

counterevidence: Novices carry a higher injury incidence per hour than recreational runners (Videbaek 2015).
